title: The Wrong Winners: Anti-Corporate Animus and Attitudes Towards Trade

selected_claim.evidence_location: Table 3, “Mediation” section; the mediator is the survey item: “International trade gives corporations more political power at the expense of ordinary people.”
selected_claim.evidence_summary: The adjusted causal mediation analysis reports a negative, statistically significant average causal mediation effect through the socio-political inequality mediator (−0.05** for both trade openness and trade agreements). The paper says this belief is linked to greater hostility toward trade. This supports l4 as an adjusted mediator–outcome pathway estimate, rather than as the effect of a randomized exposure. The table does not report a standalone mediator coefficient.
selected_claim.x: Respondent agreement with the statement “International trade gives corporations more political power at the expense of ordinary people” (five-point agreement scale).
selected_claim.y: Respondent attitude toward (1) the US becoming more open to international trade and (2) the US making free trade agreements with other countries, each measured on a five-point oppose-to-favor scale.
selected_claim.target_population: U.S. adults surveyed through YouGov Omnibus, January 28–February 2, 2022.
selected_claim.adjustment_description: In the mediation analysis, the outcome models adjust for randomized treatment assignment (the big-firms-win versus competitive-industries-win prompt) and the measured controls listed for the mediation models. The mediator itself is not randomized; the paper explicitly notes that the mediator–outcome relationship is estimated observationally and depends on an unconfoundedness assumption.
selected_claim.mixed_methods_boundary: The paper’s main treatment comparison is randomized and is not the focal claim. l4 instead corresponds to the person-level mediator in the separate mediation analysis: respondents’ measured belief about trade and corporate political power is related to their measured trade attitudes in adjusted outcome models. The paper cautions that the mediator–outcome relationship is observational and requires an unconfoundedness assumption.

evidence_summary: The focal paper examines whether concern that international trade gives corporations greater political power at ordinary people's expense is associated with opposition to greater U.S. trade openness and free trade agreements. The paper also uses a randomized big-firms-win versus competitive-industries-win prompt in a mediation analysis. The mediator–outcome relationship is observational and relies on an unconfoundedness assumption. The supplied claim gives no effect estimates or detailed findings, so none are asserted here.

limitations: The exposure source category yielded only the focal corporate-power-concern variable in classification, so snapshot coverage of comparable measures is sparse.
The focal outcomes are captured through trade-openness and trade-agreement attitudes; the supplied claim does not establish coverage of any further trade-policy endpoints.
The mediator–outcome relationship is not randomized and depends on the authors' stated unconfoundedness assumption.
No additional author caveats or numerical findings were provided in the supplied claim.
